## 09:10–10:10 · §1. Quarto basics (60 min)

**Aim.** Every student has a working Quarto project with `_quarto.yml`
and an `index.qmd` that renders.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 10 (`10-publish.qmd`).

### 1.1 Intro (10 min)

Key points:

- **Quarto** is the next-generation R Markdown. It takes a `.qmd` file
  (narrative + code) and renders it to HTML, PDF, Word, EPUB, or a
  website.
- A **Quarto document** = one `.qmd` file. Good for a single report.
- A **Quarto project** = a folder with a `_quarto.yml` config + one or
  more `.qmd` files. Needed for websites, books, blogs, or when you
  want more control over output location.
- The anatomy of a `.qmd` file:
  1. YAML header (title, author, format options) — between `---` lines
  2. Markdown narrative (headings, text, lists, links)
  3. Code chunks (R code that executes when you render)
- **Visual editor vs source editor.** RStudio has both. Visual is
  friendlier for the narrative; source gives you full control. Switch
  with the toggle in the top-right of the editor pane. We'll use source.

### 1.2 Students try (15 min)

Prompt on screen:

> **In your R-4-HASS project:**
>
> 1. File → New File → Text File. Save it as `_quarto.yml` in the
>    project root (not in `scripts/`, not in `data/` — the top level).
>
> 2. Paste this into `_quarto.yml`:
>
>    ```yaml
>    project:
>      type: website
>      output-dir: docs
>
>    website:
>      title: "My R-4-HASS Portfolio"
>      navbar:
>        left:
>          - href: index.qmd
>            text: Home
>
>    format:
>      html:
>        theme: cosmo
>        toc: true
>    ```
>
> 3. File → New File → Quarto Document. Title: "Alice in Wonderland —
>    a corpus analysis". Save it as `index.qmd` in the project root.
>
> 4. Delete the template content below the YAML.
>
> 5. Add a one-sentence intro:
>
>    ```
>    This document reports a short corpus analysis of Lewis Carroll's
>    *Alice's Adventures in Wonderland* using the quanteda package.
>    ```
>
> 6. Click **Render** (the blue arrow icon at the top of the editor).

The Render button triggers Quarto to process the file. First render
takes 10–20 seconds. A preview opens.

### 1.3 Demo (20 min)

Project on screen. Build up `index.qmd` to show the main pieces:

````markdown
---
title: "Alice in Wonderland: a corpus analysis"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    theme: cosmo
---

# Introduction

Lewis Carroll's *Alice's Adventures in Wonderland* (1865) is a classic
of children's literature. In this document I apply simple corpus-
analytic methods to the text to illustrate what quantitative analysis
can reveal about even familiar material.

The analysis uses the `quanteda` package [@benoit2018quanteda].

# Methods

```{{r setup}}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(quanteda)
library(quanteda.textstats)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)

alice_raw <- readRDS(here::here("data", "alice.rda"))
```

The text was split into chapters, tokenised, and English stopwords
were removed before frequency analysis.

```{{r prepare}}
alice_corpus <- corpus(paste(alice_raw, collapse = " "))
alice_tokens <- tokens(alice_corpus,
                        remove_punct = TRUE,
                        remove_numbers = TRUE) |>
  tokens_remove(stopwords("english"))
alice_dfm <- dfm(alice_tokens)
```

# Results

The top 15 content words in Alice are shown in @fig-freq.

```{{r}}
#| label: fig-freq
#| fig-cap: "Fifteen most frequent content words in Alice."
#| echo: false

freq <- textstat_frequency(alice_dfm) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  head(15)

ggplot(freq, aes(x = reorder(feature, frequency), y = frequency)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Frequency") +
  theme_bw()
```

# Discussion

The predominance of character names (*alice*, *queen*, *king*) and
dialogue markers (*said*, *thought*) reflects the novel's narrative
style: dialogue-heavy, character-driven.
````

Talking points while typing:

- YAML keys are indented with 2 spaces, no tabs
- Code chunks start with ```` ```{r} ```` and end with ```` ``` ````
- Chunk options use the `#|` prefix (new Quarto syntax); older R
  Markdown used chunk headers like ```` ```{r setup, message = FALSE} ```` — both work but `#|` is preferred
- `#| echo: false` hides the code; the output still shows
- `#| label: fig-freq` plus `fig-cap:` lets you cross-reference the
  figure elsewhere with `@fig-freq`

### 1.4 Exercise (15 min)

> **Task.** Starting from the demo above as a template:
>
> 1. Change the title to something that makes sense for your own analysis
> 2. Add your name to `author:`
> 3. Add an Introduction section (2–3 sentences)
> 4. Add a Methods section with a code chunk that loads `library(dplyr)`
>    and reads some data (either the Alice data or your own)
> 5. Render. Verify it looks right in the preview.
>
> Commit `_quarto.yml` and `index.qmd` to Git.

Common failure modes:

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| "Could not find Quarto" | Quarto not installed | Visit quarto.org/docs/get-started/, install, restart RStudio |
| YAML error on render | Indentation wrong (tabs vs spaces) | Replace tabs with 2 spaces |
| Code chunk doesn't run | Package not loaded or data missing | Add `library(...)` to setup chunk |
| Preview opens then closes | Browser blocking local HTML | Use the Viewer pane in RStudio instead |

## 10:25–11:40 · §2. Writing an analytical document (75 min)

**Aim.** Every student has a complete short analytical document with
intro, methods, results (with figures and tables), and discussion.
This is the template they'll adapt for their Prüfungsleistung.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 10, document-authoring section.

### 2.1 Intro (10 min)

Key points:

- An analytical document is just a formal version of a lab notebook:
  intro (what question), methods (how you did it), results (what you
  found), discussion (what it means).
- The point of Quarto for this: the code, the output, and the
  narrative are in one file. Change the data, re-render, everything
  updates. That's reproducibility in practice.
- Minimal structure for the Prüfungsleistung submission:
  - Introduction (1–2 paragraphs)
  - Methods (1 paragraph + code chunks)
  - Results (1–2 figures + 1 table, with code)
  - Discussion (1 paragraph)
- Length targets by Studiengang are in the course README — your task
  today is to build the shell at the shorter end, then fill it with
  your own data after the course.

### 2.2 Students try (15 min)

> Using your `index.qmd` from §1, add these section headings (each with
> a one-line placeholder beneath):
>
> ```
> # Introduction
>
> Placeholder.
>
> # Methods
>
> Placeholder.
>
> # Results
>
> Placeholder.
>
> # Discussion
>
> Placeholder.
>
> # References
>
> ::: {#refs}
> :::
> ```
>
> Render. Confirm the TOC on the left updates to show the sections.

### 2.3 Demo (30 min)

Build the document out piece by piece — the Alice example from §1
is a good scaffold. Add:

**A table using `flextable`:**

````markdown
```{{r}}
#| label: tbl-top10
#| tbl-cap: "Top 10 content words in Alice."
#| echo: false

library(flextable)

freq |>
  head(10) |>
  dplyr::select(feature, frequency, rank) |>
  flextable() |>
  flextable::set_table_properties(width = .5, layout = "autofit") |>
  flextable::theme_zebra()
```
````

**Cross-references:**

```markdown
As @tbl-top10 shows, *alice* and *said* dominate the frequency list.
@fig-freq visualises the same distribution.
```

**A callout:**

```markdown
::: {.callout-note}
Note that stopwords have been removed; function words like *the* and
*and* would otherwise dominate the top of the list.
:::
```

**Citations (if `references.bib` exists in the project):**

In YAML header, add:
```yaml
bibliography: references.bib
```

Then in prose:
```markdown
The analysis follows standard corpus-linguistic practice [@baker2006].
```

Talking points:

- `#| echo: false` hides the code chunk from output but keeps the
  figure/table. Useful for the Prüfungsleistung if the reader shouldn't
  see the plotting code.
- `#| echo: true` (default) shows both code and output. Useful for a
  reproducible analysis document where the code IS part of the point.
- Cross-references use `@fig-NAME`, `@tbl-NAME`, `@sec-NAME`,
  `@eq-NAME`.
- `::: {.callout-note}` creates a styled box. Variants:
  `callout-tip`, `callout-warning`, `callout-important`,
  `callout-caution`.

### 2.4 Exercise (20 min)

> **Task.** Build out your document:
>
> 1. Write a 2–3 sentence Introduction
> 2. In Methods, include a code chunk that loads the libraries you
>    used in Days 1–3 and reads your data
> 3. In Results, include at least one figure (with cross-reference)
>    and one table (with cross-reference)
> 4. Write 2–3 sentences of Discussion
> 5. Render. Verify figures and tables appear with their numbers and
>    captions.
>
> Commit the finished document to Git.

## 12:40–13:30 · §3. Rendering and output formats (50 min)

**Aim.** Every student renders their document to HTML (works) and
understands how to render to PDF (may or may not work depending on
LaTeX install). All output lands in `docs/`.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 10, rendering section.

### 3.1 Intro (10 min)

Key points:

- **Render** = run all the code, produce the output file(s). HTML is
  default and most reliable.
- Because of `output-dir: docs` in `_quarto.yml`, Quarto puts the
  rendered files in `docs/`, not in the project root. This is what
  we want for GitHub Pages.
- Multiple output formats are supported. HTML needs no extra install.
  PDF needs LaTeX (install `tinytex` once with
  `tinytex::install_tinytex()`).
- The Render button triggers whichever format is listed FIRST in
  `format:`. For multiple formats, use the Terminal:
  `quarto render index.qmd --to html` or `--to pdf`.

### 3.2 Students try (10 min)

> 1. Verify the `output-dir: docs` line is in your `_quarto.yml` under
>    `project:`
> 2. Click Render in RStudio
> 3. Open your `docs/` folder in Finder/Explorer. You should see
>    `index.html` and a `site_libs/` or `index_files/` folder with CSS
>    and JavaScript dependencies.
> 4. Open `docs/index.html` in a browser. It should look like your
>    preview, but as a standalone file.

### 3.3 Demo (15 min)

Show the Terminal rendering workflow:

```bash
# In the Terminal tab inside RStudio
quarto render                       # render whole project
quarto render index.qmd             # render one file
quarto render index.qmd --to html   # explicit format
quarto render index.qmd --to pdf    # requires LaTeX
```

Show PDF troubleshooting:

```r
# If PDF rendering fails with LaTeX errors:
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()
# Then retry quarto render --to pdf
```

Show adding multiple formats to YAML:

```yaml
format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    toc: true
  pdf:
    documentclass: article
```

Talking points:

- For your Prüfungsleistung, HTML is likely sufficient — it's what
  GitHub Pages serves, and it renders interactive content (tables,
  code folding) that PDF can't.
- PDF is nice for printing and for traditionalist readers but is
  slower to render and more fragile to produce.
- If a chunk errors during render, the whole render fails. Debug by
  running chunks interactively in RStudio first.

### 3.4 Exercise (15 min)

> **Task.**
>
> 1. Render your document to HTML (should already work)
> 2. Open `docs/index.html` in a browser — looks right?
> 3. Try adding `pdf:` to your YAML `format:` block
> 4. Render to PDF via Terminal: `quarto render index.qmd --to pdf`
> 5. If PDF fails: that's fine — install `tinytex` and try again, or
>    skip PDF and stick with HTML for the course
>
> **Stretch:** add `code-fold: true` to the YAML's `html:` block. Render.
> What changes about how code chunks are displayed?

## 13:45–15:15 · §4. Publishing to GitHub Pages (90 min)

**Aim.** Every student has their rendered document live at a public
URL at `https://THEIR_USERNAME.github.io/R-4-HASS/`.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 10, publishing section.

::: {.callout-important}
## This is the Day 4 payoff — don't let it slip past 15:15

If students don't have a live URL by 15:15, §5 (customisation) becomes
pointless. Design decisions baked in:

- Step-by-step prompt on screen (students follow exactly)
- Minimum viable Pages setup — not GitHub Actions, not custom domains
- Celebrate each student who gets live, by name — social proof pulls
  the rest along
:::

### 4.1 Intro (15 min)

Key points:

- **GitHub Pages** is a free static hosting service built into GitHub.
  Push HTML to a configured folder; GitHub serves it as a website at
  `https://USERNAME.github.io/REPO-NAME/`.
- Your Day 1 R-4-HASS repo already exists on GitHub. Today we
  configure it to serve the `docs/` folder as a website.
- Two things need to happen:
  1. The rendered HTML lives in `docs/` (done in §3)
  2. GitHub Pages is enabled in the repo settings, pointing at the
     `docs/` folder on the `main` branch
- One extra file is needed: `.nojekyll`. It's an empty file that tells
  GitHub "don't try to process these files with Jekyll" (GitHub's
  default static-site generator, which clashes with Quarto output).
- First render → push → enable Pages takes 1–3 minutes to go live.
  Subsequent re-renders are instant once Pages is enabled: push, wait a
  minute, refresh.

### 4.2 Students try (20 min)

> **Step 1: Create `.nojekyll` in your project root.**
>
> In RStudio Terminal:
>
> ```bash
> touch .nojekyll
> ```
>
> (On Windows, if `touch` doesn't exist, use File → New File → Text
> File, save as `.nojekyll` with nothing in it.)
>
> **Step 2: Check your `.gitignore`.**
>
> Open `.gitignore` in RStudio. If `docs/` or `/docs/` is listed,
> delete that line and save.
>
> **Step 3: Commit everything.**
>
> In RStudio's Git tab:
>
> 1. Tick `_quarto.yml`, `index.qmd`, `.nojekyll`, `.gitignore`, and
>    the whole `docs/` folder
> 2. Commit with message "Set up Quarto site for publishing"
> 3. Push to GitHub
>
> Verify on GitHub that your repo now shows a `docs/` folder with
> `index.html` inside.

### 4.3 Demo (30 min)

Project on screen. Walk through enabling GitHub Pages, slowly:

> **Step 4: Enable GitHub Pages on your repo.**
>
> 1. Go to your repo on GitHub:
>    `https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/R-4-HASS`
> 2. Click **Settings** (top right of the repo)
> 3. In the left sidebar, click **Pages**
> 4. Under "Build and deployment":
>    - **Source**: *Deploy from a branch*
>    - **Branch**: `main`
>    - **Folder**: `/docs`
> 5. Click **Save**
>
> **Step 5: Wait.**
>
> GitHub takes 1–3 minutes to build and deploy your site for the first
> time. The Pages settings page will show a URL and a status message.
>
> **Step 6: Visit your site.**
>
> Your URL will be:
> `https://YOUR_USERNAME.github.io/R-4-HASS/`
>
> If the URL shows a 404 initially: wait another minute, try again. If
> after 5 minutes it's still 404: refresh the Settings → Pages page
> and check the status.

Live-demo this on your own GitHub (do it with a test repo you've
cloned beforehand, or re-use the course repo). Students watch the URL
go from 404 to live — the social proof is important.

Common failure modes:

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| 404 after 5 minutes | Pages not configured | Settings → Pages, check source is `main` + `/docs` |
| Site shows but no styling | `.nojekyll` missing | Add it, commit, push, wait |
| Figures missing on live site | `docs/index_files/` not pushed | Check `.gitignore`, re-add and push |
| URL shows README instead of document | `index.html` not in `docs/` | Re-render; check `output-dir: docs` is in `_quarto.yml` |

### 4.4 Exercise (25 min)

> **Task.** Get your site live.
>
> 1. Verify `.nojekyll` exists
> 2. Verify `docs/index.html` exists
> 3. Verify everything is pushed to GitHub
> 4. Enable Pages per the demo
> 5. **Wait for your URL to go live.**
> 6. When it works: shout out so I can celebrate it. Open your URL
>    in the browser. Everyone in the room should see your name on
>    the board as "LIVE".
>
> **While you wait, work on these:**
>
> - Make an edit to `index.qmd` (fix a typo, improve a sentence)
> - Render
> - Commit
> - Push
> - Refresh your live URL in 1 minute — the change should appear
>
> This is the full re-publication cycle. You'll do this dozens of
> times during the Prüfungsleistung work.

Set up a whiteboard column: write student names in a "LIVE" list as
each one gets their URL working. Social reinforcement.

## 15:15–16:00 · §5. Making it yours — themes and customisation (45 min)

**Aim.** Every student personalises their site with a theme, a title,
and (optionally) a favicon. The site should feel like THEIRS, not
like a template.

**Reading / reference.** Book Ch 10, customisation section.

### 5.1 Intro (10 min)

Key points:

- Quarto comes with 25+ built-in Bootstrap themes. Change one YAML
  line, re-render, new look.
- Dark mode support is one more YAML line.
- You can customise further with CSS, but you don't need to for the
  Prüfungsleistung — pick a theme, adjust the title, done.
- The browsable list of themes:
  <https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-themes.html>

### 5.2 Students try (10 min)

> In `_quarto.yml`, under `format: html:`, try changing `theme`:
>
> ```yaml
> format:
>   html:
>     theme: cosmo        # replace with: cerulean, journal, flatly,
>                         # litera, lumen, lux, sandstone, simplex,
>                         # yeti, cosmo, united, pulse, sketchy...
>     toc: true
> ```
>
> Render. See the change. Try another theme. Settle on one you like.

### 5.3 Demo (15 min)

Show the extras students might want:

```yaml
format:
  html:
    theme:
      light: flatly
      dark: darkly
    toc: true
    toc-location: left     # or right, body
    code-fold: true        # readers can expand/collapse code
    code-tools: true       # adds a copy button
    code-copy: true
    fontsize: 1.1em
    linkcolor: steelblue
    highlight-style: github
```

For a favicon (optional):

```yaml
website:
  title: "My R-4-HASS Portfolio"
  favicon: favicon.png
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
```

Put a 32×32 or 64×64 pixel PNG in your project root called
`favicon.png`.

Talking points:

- `theme: light / dark` gives you a toggle in the top-right of the
  rendered page — users switch themselves
- Fiddling with themes is addictive — set a timebox for students, 15
  min max, don't let them lose the afternoon on this
- The `code-fold: true` option is particularly nice for the Prüfungs-
  leistung: readers who don't care about code hide it; readers who
  do, expand it

### 5.4 Exercise (10 min)

> **Task.**
>
> 1. Choose a theme that matches your taste
> 2. (Optional) Add a dark theme variant
> 3. Add `code-fold: true` so code chunks start hidden
> 4. Update the site title in `_quarto.yml` to something personal
> 5. Render, push, refresh your live URL, admire
>
> **If you have extra time:** make a 64×64 favicon
> (<https://favicon.io/> is a free tool) and add it to your project.

## 16:00–16:30 · Showcase + wrap-up + farewell (30 min)

**Suggested structure:**

### 16:00–16:15 · Showcase (15 min)

- Ask for volunteers (expect 5–8 hands). Project each student's URL
  on the main screen in turn. 60 seconds each.
- Point out what's different about each: topic, theme, whether they
  used their own data, structural choices.
- The purpose: everyone sees that building a published document is
  achievable. The students who were quietly stuck see what the
  achievable thing looks like.

### 16:15–16:25 · The Prüfungsleistung path (10 min)

- "What you built today is the shell. Over the next three months, you
  fill it with your own data and analysis."
- Deadline: 31 March 2027
- The three tracks (reiterate briefly, don't labour)
- Where to get help: email with `LMU` subject prefix

### 16:25–16:30 · Farewell (5 min)

- What they've done in four days: R setup → Git/GitHub → data
  wrangling → visualisation → text analytics → mixed-effects models →
  CITs → Quarto → public publishing. That's a complete reproducible
  research toolchain.
- Honest framing: "You will not retain all of this. You WILL retain
  more than you think, and when you need something back, the book is
  there."
- Thanks for the four days. Good luck with the Prüfungsleistung. See
  you on GitHub.

::: {.callout-tip}
## For your own records

Note which students have live URLs by the end of the day. These are
the students most likely to submit a Quarto document (as opposed to
Hausarbeit) for Prüfungsleistung. Useful to know when their files
land in March.
:::

## Appendix A — Risk register for Day 4

| # | Risk | Likelihood | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Quarto not installed | Medium | Pre-session email verified install; have installer bookmark ready |
| 2 | `_quarto.yml` indentation errors | High | Students pasting the yaml block; show them YAML is sensitive to tabs vs spaces |
| 3 | `output-dir: docs` not taking effect | Medium | Verify students saved `_quarto.yml` and restarted their R session |
| 4 | GitHub Pages 404 for >5 min | High | Patience — first builds genuinely take 1–3 min; after 5 min, check Settings → Pages status message |
| 5 | PDF rendering fails for everyone who tries | Very high | Pre-plan: tell students PDF is optional, HTML is the submission format |
| 6 | Student has no new GitHub commits since Day 1 (lost repo) | Low | Need to help them re-clone; worst case, create fresh repo in §4.2 |
| 7 | Student's site is live but renders a blank page | Medium | Usually missing `.nojekyll` or `_files/` folder — see §4 troubleshooting table |

## Appendix B — If you fall behind

If §1 (Quarto basics) runs past 10:30:

- Shorten §2 Intro to 5 min, cut Exercise 2.4 to steps 1–3
- Keep §3 at full 50 min — rendering is prerequisite for §4
- Protect §4 at 90 min

If §4 (publishing) runs past 15:30:

- Cut §5 to 30 min: just change theme + title + one re-render cycle
- Keep the showcase at 15 min — it's a payoff moment

If a student can't get their URL live by 15:15:

- Pair them with a classmate who IS live during §5
- They can finish at home with the book's publishing chapter
- Don't let one stuck student eat the showcase time
